results.name: trial_drift_yes_rate
results.description: Yes-rate on trials in the second half of a session (trial_index >= median) minus the first half; observed > null means people become more liberal over the session, a drift the stationary model does not produce.

results.name: partial_last_digit_match
results.description: For sets of 2+ examples whose last digits are NOT all equal, among targets not in the set and outside the set's range, yes-rate for targets sharing a last digit with at least one example minus those sharing none; observed > null means people use partial feature (digit) similarity that the all-or-nothing rule model misses.
results.code:
# name: partial_last_digit_match
# description: For sets of 2+ examples whose last digits are NOT all equal, among targets not in the set and outside the set's range, yes-rate for targets sharing a last digit with at least one example minus those sharing none; observed > null means people use partial feature (digit) similarity that the all-or-nothing rule model misses.
def test_statistic(df):
    codes, uniq = pd.factorize(df["number_set"].astype(str))
    ex = pd.Series(uniq).str.split(",", expand=True).apply(pd.to_numeric, errors="coerce").to_numpy(dtype=float)
    E = ex[codes]  # (rows, 4) examples, NaN-padded, in shown order
    t = df["target"].astype(float).to_numpy()
    y = df["rating"].astype(float).to_numpy()
    n = np.sum(~np.isnan(E), axis=1)
    ld = np.mod(E, 10)
    mixed = (n >= 2) & (np.nanmin(ld, axis=1) != np.nanmax(ld, axis=1))
    lo = np.nanmin(E, axis=1); hi = np.nanmax(E, axis=1)
    inset = np.any(E == t[:, None], axis=1)
    elig = mixed & ~inset & ((t < lo) | (t > hi))
    share = np.any(ld == np.mod(t, 10)[:, None], axis=1)
    a = elig & share; b = elig & ~share
    if a.sum() == 0 or b.sum() == 0:
        return 0.0
    return float(y[a].mean() - y[b].mean())

results.name: between_set_yes_rate_sd
results.description: Standard deviation across distinct sets of the per-set yes-rate (sets with >= 20 responses); observed > null means human generalization breadth varies more across sets than the model predicts (some sets far broader/narrower), observed < null means the model over-differentiates sets.

results.name: parity_match_in_range
results.description: For sets of 2+ examples that all share one parity, among targets strictly inside the set's range and not in the set, yes-rate for parity-matching targets minus parity-mismatching ones; observed > null means people weight parity within an interval more than the model does (observed < null: less).
results.code:
# name: parity_match_in_range
# description: For sets of 2+ examples that all share one parity, among targets strictly inside the set's range and not in the set, yes-rate for parity-matching targets minus parity-mismatching ones; observed > null means people weight parity within an interval more than the model does (observed < null: less).
def test_statistic(df):
    codes, uniq = pd.factorize(df["number_set"].astype(str))
    ex = pd.Series(uniq).str.split(",", expand=True).apply(pd.to_numeric, errors="coerce").to_numpy(dtype=float)
    E = ex[codes]  # (rows, 4) examples, NaN-padded, in shown order
    t = df["target"].astype(float).to_numpy()
    y = df["rating"].astype(float).to_numpy()
    n = np.sum(~np.isnan(E), axis=1)
    par = np.mod(E, 2)
    pmin = np.nanmin(par, axis=1); pmax = np.nanmax(par, axis=1)
    same = (n >= 2) & (pmin == pmax)
    lo = np.nanmin(E, axis=1); hi = np.nanmax(E, axis=1)
    inset = np.any(E == t[:, None], axis=1)
    inr = same & (t > lo) & (t < hi) & ~inset
    match = inr & (np.mod(t, 2) == pmin)
    mis = inr & (np.mod(t, 2) != pmin)
    if match.sum() == 0 or mis.sum() == 0:
        return 0.0
    return float(y[match].mean() - y[mis].mean())

results.name: outside_range_distance_slope
results.description: Among targets outside the [min,max] range of their set, the OLS slope of yes against log(1 + distance to the nearest example); observed more negative than null means human generalization falls off with distance more steeply than the model predicts (less negative = flatter).
results.code:
# name: outside_range_distance_slope
# description: Among targets outside the [min,max] range of their set, the OLS slope of yes against log(1 + distance to the nearest example); observed more negative than null means human generalization falls off with distance more steeply than the model predicts (less negative = flatter).
def test_statistic(df):
    codes, uniq = pd.factorize(df["number_set"].astype(str))
    ex = pd.Series(uniq).str.split(",", expand=True).apply(pd.to_numeric, errors="coerce").to_numpy(dtype=float)
    E = ex[codes]  # (rows, 4) examples, NaN-padded, in shown order
    t = df["target"].astype(float).to_numpy()
    y = df["rating"].astype(float).to_numpy()
    n = np.sum(~np.isnan(E), axis=1)
    lo = np.nanmin(E, axis=1); hi = np.nanmax(E, axis=1)
    out = (t < lo) | (t > hi)
    d = np.log1p(np.nanmin(np.abs(E - t[:, None]), axis=1))
    x, yy = d[out], y[out]
    if len(x) < 3 or np.var(x) == 0:
        return 0.0
    return float(np.cov(x, yy, bias=True)[0, 1] / np.var(x))

results.name: singleton_near_far_contrast
results.description: For one-example sets, yes-rate for targets within 10 of the example (excluding the example itself) minus yes-rate for targets more than 30 away; observed > null means people generalize from a single example more locally (similarity-based) than the model's rule/interval mixture plus guessing predicts.
results.code:
# name: singleton_near_far_contrast
# description: For one-example sets, yes-rate for targets within 10 of the example (excluding the example itself) minus yes-rate for targets more than 30 away; observed > null means people generalize from a single example more locally (similarity-based) than the model's rule/interval mixture plus guessing predicts.
def test_statistic(df):
    codes, uniq = pd.factorize(df["number_set"].astype(str))
    ex = pd.Series(uniq).str.split(",", expand=True).apply(pd.to_numeric, errors="coerce").to_numpy(dtype=float)
    E = ex[codes]  # (rows, 4) examples, NaN-padded, in shown order
    t = df["target"].astype(float).to_numpy()
    y = df["rating"].astype(float).to_numpy()
    n = np.sum(~np.isnan(E), axis=1)
    s = n == 1
    d = np.abs(E[:, 0] - t)
    near = s & (d > 0) & (d <= 10)
    far = s & (d > 30)
    if near.sum() == 0 or far.sum() == 0:
        return 0.0
    return float(y[near].mean() - y[far].mean())

results.name: interior_yes_rate_large_sets
results.description: Yes-rate for targets strictly inside the [min,max] range of 3-4 example sets (not themselves examples); observed < null means people fill in the gaps between examples less than the model's interval hypotheses imply (observed > null: more).

def test_statistic(df):

    E = ex[codes]  # (rows, 4) examples, NaN-padded, in shown order
    t = df["target"].astype(float).to_numpy()

    n = np.sum(~np.isnan(E), axis=1)
    lo = np.nanmin(E, axis=1); hi = np.nanmax(E, axis=1)
    inset = np.any(E == t[:, None], axis=1)
    m = (n >= 3) & (t > lo) & (t < hi) & ~inset

    return float(y[m].mean())

results.name: first_vs_last_example_proximity
results.description: In sets of 2+ examples, yes-rate for targets within 5 of the first-shown example (but more than 5 from the last-shown) minus targets within 5 of the last-shown (but more than 5 from the first), excluding set members; observed > 0 relative to null means a primacy effect (observed < null: recency) that the order-blind model cannot produce.
results.code:
# name: first_vs_last_example_proximity
# description: In sets of 2+ examples, yes-rate for targets within 5 of the first-shown example (but more than 5 from the last-shown) minus targets within 5 of the last-shown (but more than 5 from the first), excluding set members; observed > 0 relative to null means a primacy effect (observed < null: recency) that the order-blind model cannot produce.
def test_statistic(df):
    codes, uniq = pd.factorize(df["number_set"].astype(str))
    ex = pd.Series(uniq).str.split(",", expand=True).apply(pd.to_numeric, errors="coerce").to_numpy(dtype=float)
    E = ex[codes]  # (rows, 4) examples, NaN-padded, in shown order
    t = df["target"].astype(float).to_numpy()
    y = df["rating"].astype(float).to_numpy()
    n = np.sum(~np.isnan(E), axis=1)
    idx = np.clip(n - 1, 0, None).astype(int)
    first = E[:, 0]
    last = E[np.arange(len(E)), idx]
    inset = np.any(E == t[:, None], axis=1)
    m = (n >= 2) & ~inset
    nf = np.abs(t - first) <= 5; nl = np.abs(t - last) <= 5
    a = m & nf & ~nl; b = m & nl & ~nf
    if a.sum() == 0 or b.sum() == 0:
        return 0.0
    return float(y[a].mean() - y[b].mean())
